overview.text: In propositional logic, an implication “if p, then q” has a contrapositive: “if not q, then not p.” It reverses the order of the two parts and negates both. Unlike the converse (“if q, then p”), it has exactly the same truth value as the original for every assignment of truth values, so they are true or false together. This equivalence makes contraposition a useful proof strategy: to establish an implication, prove its contrapositive instead. For example, “if an integer’s square is even, then the integer is even” is equivalent to “if the integer is odd, then its square is odd.” Carefully negating both parts matters; merely reversing them gives the converse, which is not generally equivalent.

key_facts.text: For “if p, then q,” form the contrapositive by reversing the parts and negating each: “if not q, then not p.”
An implication and its contrapositive are logically equivalent: they share the same truth value in every case.
The converse, “if q, then p,” only switches the parts; it is not generally equivalent to the original implication.
A proof by contrapositive proves the reversed-and-negated implication directly, then uses its equivalence to conclude the original implication.
For integers, “if the square is even, then the integer is even” has the equivalent contrapositive “if the integer is odd, then its square is odd.”
